chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter introduces the concept of similarity in geometry, focusing on the properties of triangles, proportionality theorems, and the relationship between the areas of similar figures.
learning_objectives: Find the ratio of areas of two triangles based on base and height.
Understand and apply the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse.
Apply the property of an angle bisector of a triangle.
Understand the property of intercepts made by three parallel lines on transversals.
Identify similar triangles using AAA, AA, SAS, and SSS tests.
Apply the theorem of areas of similar triangles.

content_chunks.topic: Ratio of areas of two triangles
content_chunks.heading: Ratio of areas of two triangles
content_chunks.explanation: The ratio of the areas of two triangles is equal to the ratio of the products of their bases and corresponding heights. If the base of a triangle is $b_1$ and height is $h_1$, and for another triangle the base is $b_2$ and height is $h_2$, then the ratio of their areas is $\frac{b_1 \times h_1}{b_2 \times h_2}$.
key_points: The ratio of the areas of two triangles with equal heights is equal to the ratio of their corresponding bases.
The ratio of the areas of two triangles with equal bases is equal to the ratio of their corresponding heights.

formulas.name: General Ratio of Areas
formulas.description: Ratio of areas of any two triangles.

formulas.name: Equal Heights Ratio
formulas.description: Ratio of areas when heights are equal.

formulas.name: Equal Bases Ratio
formulas.description: Ratio of areas when bases are equal.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta ABC$, $AE \perp$ seg $BC$. In $\Delta DBC$, $DF \perp$ line $BC$. If $AE = 4$ and $DF = 6$, find $\frac{A(\Delta ABC)}{A(\Delta DBC)}$.

solution_steps.step: Identify that both triangles share the same base $BC$.
Apply the property that for triangles with equal bases, areas are proportional to heights.
Substitute the given values and simplify.

practice_problems.q: Base of a triangle is 9 and height is 5. Base of another triangle is 10 and height is 6. Find the ratio of areas of these triangles.

content_chunks.heading: Basic proportionality theorem
content_chunks.explanation: If a line parallel to a side of a triangle intersects the remaining sides in two distinct points, then the line divides the sides in the same proportion.
key_points: Given: In $\Delta ABC$, line $l \parallel$ side $BC$ and line $l$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ in points $P$ and $Q$ respectively.
To prove: $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{AQ}{QC}$.

formulas.name: BPT Formula
formulas.description: Proportionality of segments created by a parallel line.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta ABC$, $DE \parallel BC$. If $DB = 5.4$ cm, $AD = 1.8$ cm, $EC = 7.2$ cm, then find $AE$.

content_chunks.heading: Converse of basic proportionality theorem
content_chunks.explanation: If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
key_points: If $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{AQ}{QC}$, then line $l \parallel$ side $BC$.

content_chunks.heading: Property of an angle bisector of a triangle
content_chunks.explanation: The bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the side opposite to the angle in the ratio of the remaining sides.
key_points: Given: In $\Delta ABC$, bisector of $\angle C$ intersects seg $AB$ in point $E$.
To prove: $\frac{AE}{EB} = \frac{CA}{CB}$.

formulas.name: Angle Bisector Theorem
formulas.description: Ratio of segments of the opposite side equals ratio of other two sides.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta PQR$, seg $RS$ bisects $\angle R$. If $PR = 15$, $RQ = 20$, $PS = 12$, then find $SQ$.

solution_steps.step: Apply the property of angle bisector.

content_chunks.heading: Property of three parallel lines and their transversals
content_chunks.explanation: The ratio of the intercepts made on a transversal by three parallel lines is equal to the ratio of the corresponding intercepts made on any other transversal by the same parallel lines.
key_points: If line $l \parallel$ line $m \parallel$ line $n$, and $t_1, t_2$ are transversals, then $\frac{AB}{BC} = \frac{PQ}{QR}$.

formulas.name: Parallel Lines Intercepts
formulas.description: Equality of ratios of intercepts on different transversals.

content_chunks.heading: Tests of similarity of triangles
content_chunks.explanation: Two triangles are similar if their corresponding angles are congruent and their corresponding sides are in proportion. Specific tests can confirm similarity with fewer conditions.
key_points: AAA Test: Three corresponding angles are congruent.
AA Test: Two corresponding angles are congruent (sufficient because the third must then be congruent).
SAS Test: Two pairs of corresponding sides are in proportion and the included angles are congruent.
SSS Test: Three pairs of corresponding sides are in proportion.

content_chunks.heading: Theorem of areas of similar triangles
content_chunks.explanation: When two triangles are similar, the ratio of areas of those triangles is equal to the ratio of the squares of their corresponding sides.
key_points: If $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR$, then $\frac{A(\Delta ABC)}{A(\Delta PQR)} = \frac{AB^2}{PQ^2} = \frac{BC^2}{QR^2} = \frac{AC^2}{PR^2}$.

formulas.name: Areas of Similar Triangles
formulas.description: Ratio of areas equals ratio of squares of corresponding sides.

worked_example.problem: $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR$, $A(\Delta ABC) = 16$, $A(\Delta PQR) = 25$, find the ratio $\frac{AB}{PQ}$.

solution_steps.step: Apply the theorem of areas of similar triangles.
Take the square root of both sides.

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter explores the fundamental Pythagoras theorem, its converse, properties of special right-angled triangles, the geometric mean theorem, and the Apollonius theorem for medians.
learning_objectives: Identify and verify Pythagorean triplets.
Understand similarity in right-angled triangles.
Apply the theorem of geometric mean.
Prove and apply Pythagoras theorem and its converse.
Solve problems using properties of 30°-60°-90° and 45°-45°-90° triangles.
Understand and apply Apollonius theorem.

content_chunks.heading: Pythagoras theorem
content_chunks.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the remaining two sides. In $\Delta PQR$ where $\angle PQR = 90^\circ$, $PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2$.
key_points: Applies only to right-angled triangles.
The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and is the longest side.

formulas.name: Pythagoras Formula
formulas.description: Where c is the hypotenuse and a, b are the other two sides.

worked_example.problem: In a right-angled triangle, sides making the right angle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.

content_chunks.heading: Pythagorean Triplet
content_chunks.explanation: In a triplet of natural numbers, if the square of the largest number is equal to the sum of the squares of the remaining two numbers, then the triplet is called a Pythagorean triplet. For example, (11, 60, 61) is a triplet because $11^2 + 60^2 = 121 + 3600 = 3721 = 61^2$.
key_points: Triplets consist of natural numbers.
Formula for generating triplets: $[(a^2 + b^2), (a^2 - b^2), (2ab)]$ where $a > b$.

practice_problems.q: Identify if (3, 5, 4) is a Pythagorean triplet.

content_chunks.heading: Property of 30°-60°-90° and 45°-45°-90° triangles
content_chunks.explanation:
These are properties of specific right-angled triangles that allow finding side lengths based on the hypotenuse. 
1. 30°-60°-90°: Side opposite 30° is $\frac{1}{2} \times$ hypotenuse; side opposite 60° is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times$ hypotenuse. 
2. 45°-45°-90°: Each perpendicular side is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times$ hypotenuse.
key_points: 30°-60°-90° is a scalene right triangle.
45°-45°-90° is an isosceles right triangle.

formulas.name: 30° Side
formulas.description: Side opposite 30 degrees.

formulas.name: 60° Side
formulas.description: Side opposite 60 degrees.

formulas.name: 45° Side
formulas.description: Sides of an isosceles right triangle.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta LMN$, $\angle L = 30^\circ, \angle N = 60^\circ, \angle M = 90^\circ$. If $LN = 6$ cm, find $MN$ and $LM$.

content_chunks.heading: Similarity and right angled triangle
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: In a right-angled triangle, if the altitude is drawn to the hypotenuse, then the two triangles formed are similar to the original triangle and to each other.
key_points: Given: In $\Delta ABC$, $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, seg $BD \perp$ seg $AC$.
Result: $\Delta ADB \sim \Delta BDC \sim \Delta ABC$.

content_chunks.heading: Theorem of geometric mean
content_chunks.explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the perpendicular segment to the hypotenuse from the opposite vertex is the geometric mean of the segments into which the hypotenuse is divided.
key_points: If $QS$ is the altitude to hypotenuse $PR$, then $QS^2 = PS \times SR$.

formulas.name: Geometric Mean Theorem
formulas.description: Altitude squared equals product of hypotenuse segments.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta PQR$, $\angle PQR = 90^\circ$, seg $QN \perp$ seg $PR$. If $PN = 9, NR = 16$, find $QN$.

content_chunks.heading: Converse of Pythagoras theorem
content_chunks.explanation: In a triangle, if the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the remaining two sides, then the triangle is a right-angled triangle.
key_points: Used to verify if a triangle is right-angled given its side lengths.

worked_example.problem: State if $\Delta LMN$ with $l=5, m=13, n=12$ is right-angled.
worked_example.answer: Yes, it is a right-angled triangle.

content_chunks.heading: Apollonius theorem
content_chunks.explanation: In $\Delta ABC$, if $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, then $AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AM^2 + 2BM^2$. This theorem relates the sides of a triangle to its median.
key_points: Requires a median (segment from vertex to midpoint of opposite side).
Useful for finding the length of a median or a missing side.

formulas.name: Apollonius Formula
formulas.description: Relates sides and median.

worked_example.problem: In $\Delta PQR$, seg $PM$ is a median. $PM = 9$ and $PQ^2 + PR^2 = 290$. Find $QR$.

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter covers the properties of circles, including tangents, secants, touching circles, arcs, inscribed angles, cyclic quadrilaterals, and theorems related to intersecting chords.
learning_objectives: Understand circles passing through one, two, and three points.
Learn the properties of secants and tangents.
Apply the Tangent Theorem and its converse.
Understand the Tangent Segment Theorem.
Identify and solve problems related to touching circles.
Measure arcs and understand central angles.
Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem and its corollaries.
Understand the properties of cyclic quadrilaterals.
Apply theorems of internal and external division of chords.
Apply the Tangent Secant Segments Theorem.

content_chunks.heading: Circles passing through one, two, three points
content_chunks.explanation:
The number of circles that can be drawn through a set of points depends on their arrangement: 
1. Infinite circles can pass through a single point. 
2. Infinite circles can pass through two distinct points. 
3. There is a unique circle passing through three non-collinear points. 
4. No circle can pass through three collinear points.
key_points: A unique circle passes through three non-collinear points.
Collinear points cannot lie on the same circle.

content_chunks.heading: Secant and tangent
content_chunks.explanation:
A line and a circle in the same plane can have different relationships: 
1. Tangent: A line that intersects the circle at exactly one point (point of contact). 
2. Secant: A line that intersects the circle at two distinct points.
key_points: Tangent has one common point with the circle.
Secant has two common points with the circle.

content_chunks.heading: Tangent theorem
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: A tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
key_points: Radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.
This is a fundamental property used in many circle proofs.

formulas.name: Tangent Perpendicularity
formulas.description: At the point of contact, the angle is 90 degrees.

worked_example.problem: In a circle with centre C and radius 6 cm, line AB is a tangent at A. Find d(C, line AB).

solution_steps.step: By tangent theorem, the radius CA is perpendicular to tangent AB.
The distance of the centre from the tangent is the radius.

content_chunks.heading: Converse of tangent theorem
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: A line perpendicular to a radius at its point on the circle is a tangent to the circle.
key_points: Used to prove a line is a tangent.

content_chunks.heading: Tangent segment theorem
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: Tangent segments drawn from an external point to a circle are congruent.
key_points: If P is an external point and PA, PB are tangents, then $PA = PB$.
The segments are equal in length.

formulas.name: Tangent Segment Equality
formulas.description: Lengths of tangents from an external point D to points P and Q.

worked_example.problem: From point R, seg RM and seg RN are tangent segments to a circle with centre O. If OR = 10 cm and radius = 5 cm, find the length of each tangent segment.

content_chunks.heading: Touching circles
content_chunks.explanation:
Two circles in the same plane are said to be touching if they intersect at exactly one point. 
1. Externally touching: The distance between centers is the sum of their radii ($d = r_1 + r_2$). 
2. Internally touching: The distance between centers is the difference of their radii ($d = |r_1 - r_2|$).
key_points: Theorem: If two circles touch each other, their point of contact lies on the line joining their centres.

formulas.name: Distance (External)
formulas.description: Distance between centers of externally touching circles.

formulas.name: Distance (Internal)
formulas.description: Distance between centers of internally touching circles.

worked_example.problem: Two circles having radii 3.5 cm and 4.8 cm touch each other internally. Find the distance between their centres.

content_chunks.heading: Arc of a circle and Central angle
content_chunks.explanation:
A secant divides a circle into two arcs. 
1. Minor Arc: The arc on the side without the centre (usually). 
2. Major Arc: The arc on the side containing the centre. 
3. Semicircle: Arc formed by a diameter. 
Central Angle: An angle whose vertex is the centre of the circle. The measure of a minor arc is equal to the measure of its corresponding central angle.
key_points: Measure of minor arc = measure of central angle.
Measure of major arc = $360^\circ$ - measure of minor arc.
Measure of semicircle = $180^\circ$.
Measure of complete circle = $360^\circ$.

content_chunks.heading: Congruence of arcs
content_chunks.explanation:
Two arcs are congruent if their measures and radii are equal. 
Theorem: The chords corresponding to congruent arcs of a circle are congruent. 
Theorem: Corresponding arcs of congruent chords of a circle are congruent.
key_points: Congruent arcs $\Rightarrow$ Congruent chords.
Congruent chords $\Rightarrow$ Congruent arcs.

content_chunks.heading: Inscribed angle theorem
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: The measure of an inscribed angle is half of the measure of the arc intercepted by it.
key_points: Inscribed angle vertex is on the circle.
Intercepted arc is in the interior of the angle.
Corollary 1: Angles inscribed in the same arc are congruent.
Corollary 2: Angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle ($90^\circ$).

formulas.name: Inscribed Angle Formula
formulas.description: Angle is half the intercepted arc.

worked_example.problem: In a circle, chord AB is equal to the radius. Find the measure of the angle inscribed in the major arc.

solution_steps.step: Since chord AB = radius, $\Delta OAB$ is equilateral.
The measure of minor arc AB is equal to the central angle.
The inscribed angle is half the intercepted arc.

content_chunks.heading: Theorem of cyclic quadrilateral
content_chunks.explanation:
Theorem: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (sum to $180^\circ$). 
Corollary: An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is congruent to the angle opposite to its adjacent interior angle.
key_points: A quadrilateral is cyclic if all its vertices lie on a circle.
Converse: If a pair of opposite angles is supplementary, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

formulas.name: Cyclic Quad Property
formulas.description: Opposite angles sum.

worked_example.problem: In cyclic c MRPN, $\angle R = (5x - 13)^\circ$ and $\angle N = (4x + 4)^\circ$. Find measures of $\angle R$ and $\angle N$.

solution_steps.step: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

content_chunks.heading: Theorems of internal and external division of chords
content_chunks.explanation:
1. Internal Division: If two chords intersect inside a circle, the product of the segments of one chord equals the product of the segments of the other. 
2. External Division: If two secants intersect outside a circle, the product of the whole secant and its external part is constant for both secants.
key_points: Internal: $AE \times EB = CE \times ED$.
External: $AE \times EB = CE \times ED$ (where E is the external intersection point).

formulas.name: Chord Segment Product
formulas.description: Applies to both internal and external intersection.

worked_example.problem: Chords MN and RS intersect at P inside the circle. If $PR = 6, PS = 4, MN = 11$, find $PN$.

content_chunks.heading: Tangent secant segments theorem
content_chunks.explanation: Theorem: If a tangent and a secant intersect in the exterior of a circle, then the product of the segments of the secant is equal to the square of the tangent segment.
key_points: If E is an external point, ET is a tangent, and EAB is a secant, then $EA \times EB = ET^2$.

formulas.name: Tangent-Secant Formula
formulas.description: Product of secant segments equals square of tangent.

worked_example.problem: In a figure, seg PS is a tangent segment and line PR is a secant. If $PQ = 3.6$ and $QR = 6.4$, find $PS$.

solution_steps.step: Identify secant segments: $PQ = 3.6, PR = PQ + QR = 3.6 + 6.4 = 10$.

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter focuses on the practical application of geometry to construct similar triangles and tangents to circles under various conditions.
learning_objectives: Construct a triangle similar to a given triangle with a specific ratio of sides.
Construct similar triangles when vertices are distinct.
Construct similar triangles when one vertex is common.
Construct a tangent to a circle at a point on the circle using the centre.
Construct a tangent to a circle at a point on the circle without using the centre.
Construct tangents to a circle from a point outside the circle.

content_chunks.heading: Construction of Similar Triangles (Distinct Vertices)
content_chunks.explanation: To construct a triangle similar to a given triangle when the vertices are distinct, we first use the property of similarity (corresponding sides are in proportion) to calculate the lengths of the sides of the new triangle. Once the side lengths are known, the triangle is constructed using standard methods.
key_points: Identify the given ratio of corresponding sides.
Calculate the lengths of all three sides of the new triangle using the proportionality equation.
Construct the first triangle with given measures and the second with calculated measures.

formulas.name: Proportionality of Sides
formulas.description: Used to find unknown side lengths of a similar triangle.

worked_example.problem: $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR$. In $\Delta ABC$, $AB = 5.4$ cm, $BC = 4.2$ cm, $AC = 6.0$ cm. Ratio $AB:PQ = 3:2$. Construct both triangles.
worked_example.answer: Construct $\Delta ABC$ with sides 5.4, 4.2, 6.0 and $\Delta PQR$ with sides 3.6, 2.8, 4.0.

content_chunks.heading: Construction of Similar Triangles (Common Vertex)
content_chunks.explanation: When two similar triangles have a common vertex, they can be constructed on the same base line. We use a ray at an acute angle to divide the base into equal parts according to the given ratio. Parallel lines are then drawn to complete the similar triangle.
key_points: One vertex is shared between the two triangles.
Draw a ray from the common vertex at an acute angle to the base.
Mark equal parts on the ray based on the larger number in the ratio.
Draw parallel lines using the Basic Proportionality Theorem principle.

worked_example.problem: Construct $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta A'BC'$ such that $AB:A'B = 5:3$ and $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta A'BC'$.

solution_steps.step: Draw a ray from $B$ and mark 5 equal points $T_1, T_2, T_3, T_4, T_5$.
Join $T_5$ to $C$. Draw a line through $T_3$ parallel to $T_5C$ to intersect $BC$ at $C'$.
Draw a line through $C'$ parallel to $AC$ to intersect $AB$ at $A'$.

worked_example.answer: $\Delta A'BC'$ is the required similar triangle.

content_chunks.heading: Tangent at a point on the circle (Using Centre)
content_chunks.explanation: To construct a tangent at a point $P$ on a circle with centre $C$, we draw the radius $CP$ and extend it to form a line. Then, we construct a perpendicular to this line at point $P$. This perpendicular line is the required tangent.
key_points: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Extend the radius to facilitate the perpendicular construction.

content_chunks.heading: Tangent at a point on the circle (Without Using Centre)
content_chunks.explanation: This method uses the 'Tangent-Secant Angle Theorem' (or Alternate Segment Theorem). We draw a chord through the point of contact and an inscribed angle in the alternate segment. By constructing an angle at the point of contact congruent to the inscribed angle, we obtain the tangent.
key_points: Draw a chord $CB$ and an inscribed $\angle CAB$.
Construct $\angle BCD$ at point $C$ such that $\angle BCD \cong \angle CAB$.
Line $CD$ is the tangent.

content_chunks.heading: Tangents from a point outside the circle
content_chunks.explanation: To draw tangents from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, we find the midpoint $M$ of segment $OP$. A circle drawn with centre $M$ and radius $OM$ intersects the original circle at two points, $A$ and $B$. Lines $PA$ and $PB$ are the required tangents.
key_points: Two tangents can be drawn from an external point.
The construction relies on the property that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
The points of intersection $A$ and $B$ ensure that $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$.

worked_example.problem: Construct tangents to a circle with centre $O$ and radius 3.5 cm from a point $P$ at a distance 5.7 cm from the centre.

solution_steps.step: Draw the circle and locate point $P$ such that $OP = 5.7$ cm.
Draw the perpendicular bisector of $OP$ to find midpoint $M$.
Draw a circle with centre $M$ and radius $OM$. Mark intersection points $A$ and $B$.

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter introduces coordinate geometry concepts including the distance formula, section formula, midpoint formula, and centroid formula, as well as the concept of the slope of a line.
learning_objectives: Calculate the distance between any two points on an axis or in the XY plane.
Determine if three points are collinear using the distance formula or slope.
Apply the section formula to find the coordinates of a point dividing a segment in a given ratio.
Use the midpoint formula to find the center of a line segment.
Calculate the coordinates of the centroid of a triangle.
Understand the concept of the slope of a line and its relationship with trigonometric ratios.

content_chunks.heading: Distance between points on an axis
content_chunks.explanation: To find the distance between two points on the same axis, we subtract the smaller coordinate from the larger one. For points on the X-axis, $d(A, B) = x_2 - x_1$ (where $x_2 > x_1$). For points on the Y-axis, $d(P, Q) = y_2 - y_1$ (where $y_2 > y_1$). If the segment joining two points is parallel to an axis, the same logic applies to the coordinates that vary.
key_points: Distance is always a positive real number.
On the X-axis, y-coordinates are zero.
On the Y-axis, x-coordinates are zero.

formulas.name: Distance on X-axis
formulas.description: Absolute difference of x-coordinates.

formulas.name: Distance on Y-axis
formulas.description: Absolute difference of y-coordinates.

worked_example.problem: Find the distance between points P(-1, 0) and R(4, 0) on the X-axis.

solution_steps.step: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

content_chunks.heading: Distance formula
content_chunks.explanation: The distance between any two points $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ in the XY plane is derived using the Pythagoras theorem. By creating a right-angled triangle with the segment $AB$ as the hypotenuse, the distance is the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences in x and y coordinates.
key_points: Coordinates of the origin are (0, 0).
Distance from origin to $P(x, y)$ is $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.

formulas.name: General Distance Formula
formulas.description: Calculates distance between any two points in a 2D plane.

worked_example.problem: Find the distance between points P(-1, 1) and Q(5, -7).

content_chunks.heading: Collinearity using distance formula
content_chunks.explanation: Three points are collinear if they lie on the same straight line. Using the distance formula, if the sum of the distances between two pairs of points is equal to the distance between the third pair, the points are collinear.
key_points: Check $d(A, B) + d(B, C) = d(A, C)$ or other combinations.

worked_example.problem: Show that points A(-3, 2), B(1, -2) and C(9, -10) are collinear.
worked_example.answer: Points A, B, and C are collinear.

content_chunks.heading: Section formula
content_chunks.explanation: The section formula is used to find the coordinates of a point $P(x, y)$ that divides a line segment joining $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ in a given ratio $m:n$.
key_points: Internal division: Point P is between A and B.
External division: Point P is outside segment AB (provided for information).

formulas.name: Section Formula (Internal)
formulas.latex: x = \frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, y = \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}
formulas.description: Coordinates of a point dividing a segment in ratio m:n.

worked_example.problem: Find coordinates of Q dividing AB in ratio 2:3 where A(3, 5) and B(7, 9).

content_chunks.heading: Co-ordinates of the midpoint of a segment
content_chunks.explanation: The midpoint formula is a special case of the section formula where the ratio $m:n$ is $1:1$. The coordinates of the midpoint are the average of the coordinates of the endpoints.
key_points: Midpoint divides the segment into two equal parts.

formulas.name: Midpoint Formula
formulas.description: Coordinates of the center point of a segment.

worked_example.problem: Find the midpoint of segment AB with A(-4, 2) and B(6, 2).

content_chunks.heading: Centroid formula
content_chunks.explanation: The centroid of a triangle is the point where its three medians intersect. It divides each median in the ratio 2:1. If the vertices of a triangle are $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2),$ and $(x_3, y_3)$, the coordinates of the centroid $G(x, y)$ are the averages of the vertices' coordinates.
key_points: Centroid is the center of mass of the triangle.
Medians are concurrent at the centroid.

formulas.name: Centroid Formula
formulas.description: Coordinates of the intersection of medians.

content_chunks.heading: Slope of a line
content_chunks.explanation: The slope (or gradient) of a line measures its steepness. For a line passing through points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$, the slope $m$ is the ratio of the difference in y-coordinates to the difference in x-coordinates. It is also defined as the tangent of the angle $\theta$ that the line makes with the positive direction of the X-axis.
key_points: Slope $m = \tan \theta$.
Slope of X-axis and lines parallel to it is 0.
Slope of Y-axis and lines parallel to it is undefined.
Parallel lines have equal slopes.

formulas.name: Slope Formula (Points)
formulas.description: Slope using two points on the line.

formulas.name: Slope Formula (Angle)
formulas.description: Slope using the angle of inclination.

worked_example.problem: Find the slope of the line passing through A(-3, 5) and B(4, -1).

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter introduces reciprocal trigonometric ratios (cosec, sec, cot), fundamental trigonometric identities, and the practical application of trigonometry in solving problems related to heights and distances using angles of elevation and depression.
learning_objectives: Define and understand cosec, sec, and cot ratios.
Learn and prove fundamental trigonometric identities.
Understand the concepts of line of vision, angle of elevation, and angle of depression.
Solve real-world problems involving heights and distances using trigonometric ratios.

content_chunks.heading: cosec, sec and cot ratios
content_chunks.explanation:
These are the reciprocal ratios of sine, cosine, and tangent. 
1. Cosecant (cosec): The multiplicative inverse or reciprocal of the sine ratio. 
2. Secant (sec): The multiplicative inverse or reciprocal of the cosine ratio. 
3. Cotangent (cot): The multiplicative inverse or reciprocal of the tangent ratio.
key_points: $\text{cosec } \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{opposite side}}$
$\text{sec } \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent side}}$
$\text{cot } \theta = \frac{1}{\tan \theta} = \frac{\text{adjacent side}}{\text{opposite side}}$
$\sin \theta \times \text{cosec } \theta = 1$
$\cos \theta \times \text{sec } \theta = 1$
$\tan \theta \times \text{cot } \theta = 1$

formulas.description: Fundamental reciprocal relationships between trigonometric ratios.

content_chunks.heading: Trigonometric identities
content_chunks.explanation: Trigonometric identities are equations involving trigonometric ratios that are true for all values of the occurring angles. They are derived using the Pythagoras theorem in a right-angled triangle.
key_points: The three fundamental identities are derived by dividing the Pythagorean equation $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ by the square of each side.
These identities are used to simplify complex trigonometric expressions and solve equations.

formulas.name: Fundamental Identity 1
formulas.description: The most basic trigonometric identity.

formulas.name: Fundamental Identity 2
formulas.description: Relates tangent and secant.

formulas.name: Fundamental Identity 3
formulas.description: Relates cotangent and cosecant.

worked_example.problem: If $\sin \theta = \frac{20}{29}$, find $\cos \theta$.

content_chunks.heading: Application of trigonometry
content_chunks.explanation: Trigonometry is used to calculate heights of objects (towers, trees) or distances (width of a river, distance of a ship) that cannot be measured directly. This involves drawing a rough sketch and identifying right-angled triangles.
key_points: Line of vision: The line joining the eye of the observer to the object viewed.
Angle of elevation: The angle between the line of vision and the horizontal line when the object is above the horizontal level.
Angle of depression: The angle between the line of vision and the horizontal line when the object is below the horizontal level.
Vertical objects like towers or trees are represented by segments perpendicular to the ground.

worked_example.problem: An observer at a distance of 10 m from a tree looks at the top of the tree. The angle of elevation is 60°. Find the height of the tree. ($\sqrt{3} = 1.73$)

solution_steps.step: Let $AB$ be the height of the tree and $BC$ be the distance from the observer. In $\Delta ABC$, $\angle B = 90^\circ$.

chapters.chapter_summary: This chapter covers the calculation of surface areas and volumes of various three-dimensional shapes, including the frustum of a cone, as well as the properties and areas of sectors and segments of a circle.
learning_objectives: Recall and apply formulas for surface area and volume of standard 3D figures.
Understand the concept of a frustum of a cone and calculate its area and volume.
Calculate the area of a sector and the length of an arc of a circle.
Understand the relationship between arc length and sector area.
Calculate the area of a segment of a circle.

content_chunks.heading: Surface Area and Volume of Three Dimensional Figures
content_chunks.explanation: A review of fundamental 3D shapes including cuboids, cubes, cylinders, cones, spheres, and hemispheres. Each figure has specific formulas for lateral/curved surface area, total surface area, and volume based on its dimensions (length, breadth, height, radius, slant height).
key_points: Cuboid: 3 dimensions (l, b, h).
Cylinder and Cone: involve radius (r) and height (h).
Sphere: only depends on radius (r).

formulas.name: Cuboid Volume
formulas.description: Volume of a cuboid.

formulas.name: Cylinder Volume
formulas.description: Volume of a cylinder.

formulas.name: Cone Slant Height
formulas.description: Relationship between height, radius, and slant height.

formulas.name: Sphere Surface Area
formulas.description: Total surface area of a sphere.

worked_example.problem: How many solid cylinders of radius 10 cm and height 6 cm can be made by melting a solid sphere of radius 30 cm?

solution_steps.step: Divide sphere volume by cylinder volume to find n.

content_chunks.heading: Frustum of a cone
content_chunks.explanation: When a cone is cut parallel to its base, the part containing the base is called a frustum. It has two circular faces with different radii ($r_1$ and $r_2$) and a height ($h$).
key_points: A frustum is a 'truncated' cone.
Common examples include buckets and drinking glasses.
$r_1$ is typically the larger radius.

formulas.name: Frustum Slant Height
formulas.description: Slant height of a frustum.

formulas.name: Frustum Curved Surface Area
formulas.description: Area of the side surface.

formulas.name: Frustum Volume
formulas.description: Capacity of a frustum.

worked_example.problem: A bucket is frustum shaped with height 28 cm and radii 15 cm and 12 cm. Find its capacity.

content_chunks.heading: Sector of a circle
content_chunks.explanation: A sector is the part of a circular region enclosed by two radii and the arc joining their endpoints. A central angle $\theta$ divides the circle into a minor sector and a major sector.
key_points: Minor sector: central angle $\theta < 180^\circ$.
Major sector: central angle $> 180^\circ$.
Area is proportional to the central angle.

formulas.name: Area of Sector
formulas.description: Calculates the area of a sector.

formulas.name: Length of Arc
formulas.description: Calculates the length of the arc bounding the sector.

formulas.name: Arc-Area Relation
formulas.description: Direct relationship between area and arc length.

worked_example.problem: Find the area of a sector with radius 21 cm and central angle 150°.

content_chunks.heading: Area of a Segment
content_chunks.explanation: A segment of a circle is the region bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc. The area of a minor segment is found by subtracting the area of the triangle formed by the radii and the chord from the area of the corresponding sector.
key_points: Area of Segment = Area of Sector - Area of Triangle.
The formula provided is specifically for $\theta \le 90^\circ$.

formulas.name: Area of Segment
formulas.description: General formula for the area of a minor segment.

worked_example.problem: Find the area of a segment if the radius is 12 cm and the central angle is 30°. ($\pi = 3.14$)
